  #Step 2 - Prompt for a multi-variable scatter plot 
     
     # Create a ggplot scatter plot using the penguins dataset. 
     # Plot bill_length_mm on the x-axis and bill_depth_mm on the y-axis.
     # Color points by species and use geom_point with size 3.
     # Add a minimal theme and clean labels.
     
     ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
       geom_point(size = 3) +
       theme_minimal() +
       labs(title = "Bill Length vs Bill Depth by Species",
            x = "Bill Length (mm)",
            y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
            color = "Species")
     
  #Step 3 - open-end comparitive plotting 
     # build a scatter plot mapping body_mass_g against flipper_length_mm, adding a linear regression trend line (geom_smooth) for each species. 
     ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
       geom_point(size = 3) +
       geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
       theme_minimal() +
       labs(title = "Body Mass vs Flipper Length by Species",
            x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
            y = "Body Mass (g)",
            color = "Species")
     
     # generate a boxplot comparing flipper_length_mm across different species, faceted by island, using custom color palettes. 
     ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
       geom_boxplot() +
       facet_wrap(~ island) +
       scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
       theme_minimal() +
       labs(title = "Flipper Length by Species and Island",
            x = "Species",
            y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
            fill = "Species")
     
     # The boxplot was choisen to compare the distribution of flipper lengths across species, while faceting by island allows for a clear comparison of how these distributions vary across different geographic locations. 
     # The custom color palette enhances visual distinction between species. 
     # While compared to the scatter plot option, information displayed where less clearly visualized compared to the boxplot.

    
     library(tidyverse)
     library(palmerpenguins)
     
     ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
       geom_boxplot() +
       facet_wrap(~ island) +
       scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
       theme_minimal() +
       labs(title = "Flipper Length by Species and Island",
            x = "Species",
            y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
            fill = "Species")

#if_else
 
 # Load tidyverse (if not already loaded)
 library(tidyverse)

 # Sample coral data
coral_monitoring <- tibble(
  site = c("Site_A", "Site_B", "Site_C"),
  depth_m = c(12, 35, 8)
)

 # Classify depth using if_else
coral_monitoring <- coral_monitoring %>% 
  mutate(zone = if_else(depth_m > 30, "Deep Reef", "Shallow Reef"))
  
 #mutate() is used to create a new column called zone, which classifies the depth of each site as either "Deep Reef" or "Shallow Reef" based on the condition specified in if_else().

 # %>% symbol is the pipe operator from the magrittr package, which is part of the tidyverse. It allows for chaining multiple operations together in a readable manner. In this case, it takes the coral_monitoring tibble and passes it to the mutate() function to create the new zone column.

 #case_when() used when you have more than two possibilities, using mutiple if_else block becomes unreadable.

coral_monitoring <- coral_monitoring %>% 
  mutate(reef_category = case_when(
    depth_m < 10  ~ "Lagoon / Flats",
    depth_m <= 30 ~ "Crest / Slope",
    depth_m > 30  ~ "Mesophotic / Deep",
    TRUE          ~ "Unclassified" # Catch-all remainder
  ))

 #Task: Using the chattr app or inline copilot, your task here is to write an R script that initialises a tibble named marine_stations containing a column for salinity with values 35, 28, 32, and 12. Use the pipe operator (%>%) and mutate() combined with case_when() to create a new column named environment_type. Classify values below 15 as "Estuarine", values between 15 and 30 as "Brackish", and values above 30 as "Marine". Run your script and verify the table structure.

marine_station <- tibble(
  salinity = c(35, 28, 32, 12)
)

marine_station <- marine_station %>%
  mutate(environment_type = case_when(
    salinity < 15 ~ "Estuarine",
    salinity >= 15 & salinity <= 30 ~ "Brackish",
    salinity > 30 ~ "Marine"
  ))

#4.5 Writing custom functions 

# Function Definition
calculate_coral_mortality <- function(initial_count, surviving_count) {
  
  # Logic safety switch using our conditional tools!
  if (initial_count <= 0) {
    stop("Initial count must be greater than zero.")
  }
  
  mortality_rate <- (initial_count - surviving_count) / initial_count
  return(mortality_rate)
}

# Utilizing your custom function
calculate_coral_mortality(initial_count = 120, surviving_count = 84)

#Task - student exercise 4: Custom Function Construction 

Instruction:Build a custom function named convert_temp_c_to_f that accepts a single argument representing temperature in Celsius. The function should perform the math conversion: F = (C * 9/5) + 32. Include a conditional safety check using an if statement that halts execution via stop() if the entered value is below absolute zero (-273.15 degrees Celsius). Test your function with both a valid temperature and an invalid value to ensure the error handling behaves as expected.

convert_temp_c_to_f <- function(temp_c) {
  # Safety check for absolute zero
  if (temp_c < -273.15) {
    stop("Temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15°C).")
  }
  
  # Conversion formula
  temp_f <- (temp_c * 9/5) + 32
  return(temp_f)
}


Challenge 1: Nested Multi-Vector Iteration
In real-world field surveys, calculations often depend on matching values across multiple lists or matrices. Read the documentation for purrr::map2_dbl(). Given a vector of raw survey counts counts <- c(15, 24, 8, 42) and a vector of species-specific scaling factors factors <- c(1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 1.1), write a mapping statement that iterates across both vectors simultaneously to return a single vector of scaled abundance values. Do not use a manual index loop.

library(purrr)
counts <- c(15, 24, 8, 42)
factors <- c(1.2, 0.8, 2.5,1.1)

scaled_abundance <- map2_dbl(counts, factors, ~ .x * .y)

Challenge 2: The Robust Data Wrangling Pipeline Function

Create a custom function named clean_and_classify_survey that handles complex data frame structures. The function must fulfill these criteria:

1) Accept a data frame and a column name threshold parameter as inputs.
2) Safely check if the specified column name exists within the passed data frame; if it does not, trigger a user-friendly error message using stop().
3) Filter out rows containing missing values (NA) within that specific column.
4) Use the pipe operator and mutate() along with a vectorised conditional (if_else() or case_when()) to append a status string variable classification based on your threshold parameter.
5) Return the cleaned, altered data frame to the global environment.

Test your custom pipeline using a mock tibble that contains at least one missing value to confirm your code handles anomalies without crashing.

clean_and_classify_survey <- function(data, column_name, threshold) {
  # Check if the specified column exists
  if (!column_name %in% colnames(data)) {
    stop(paste("Column", column_name, "does not exist in the data frame."))
  }
  
  # Filter out rows with NA in the specified column and classify based on threshold
  cleaned_data <- data %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[column_name]])) %>%
    mutate(classification = case_when(
      .data[[column_name]] < threshold ~ "Below Threshold",
      .data[[column_name]] >= threshold ~ "Above Threshold"
    ))
  
  return(cleaned_data)
}
